terms.gloss: wicked, bad (of people and what they do)
evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.297: improbī esse hominis et perfidiōsī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The everyday prose word for a bad man, the opposite of probus; improbitās is wickedness. Without a moral sense it means shameless, relentless, beyond measure: labor improbus (Verg. G. 1.146), the relentless work that conquers all (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: an evil, a harm, a misfortune
evidence: Cic. Lael. 10: nihil enim malī accidisse Scīpiōnī putō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The neuter of malus (see bad): anything bad that happens to someone, from a misfortune to a punishment. Not to be confused with mālum, an apple.

terms.gloss: abominable, heinous (of a crime or its doer)
evidence: Cic. Off. 2.51: homō nefārius et impius (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: From nefās (see wrong): stronger than improbus, what offends gods and men.

terms.gloss: wicked; as a term of abuse, you villain!
terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; Cicero does not use it of persons
evidence: Ter. Eun. 4.4.41 (Lewis & Short): ō scelestum atque audācem hominem!

phrases.english: the success of the wicked lures more of them
the wickedness of a few is a disaster for everyone
